method: Each listed item was read with its stem, all options, keyed answer(s), explanations and takeaway. Statuses are manually reasoned, not inferred from a schema or automated pass rule.
limitations: Independent AI editorial/clinical-reasoning screen; not external clinician validation or psychometric validation.
Pass applies only to the recorded content hash. New or changed content requires further review.
No comparison against proprietary examination items; originality judged from author provenance and item content.
Cross-bank learning-objective overlap remains provisional until all batches are available.
Source checks below support only the explicitly associated claims; other category references are general reading unless specifically verified.

items.assessment: Full-minute apical assessment is superior to abbreviated extrapolation or an automated rate alone for observed irregularity; meaningful symptomatic context retained.
Comparable repeat measurement addresses both scale and clothing differences; arbitrary correction or averaging cannot establish a real weight change.
Stable status and conflicting chart/report make clarification and assessment appropriate; documenting invented measured volumes or confirmed anuria would misrepresent the evidence.

proposedChanges.stem: A dehydrated adult’s creatinine rises from 70 to 145 µmol/L in two days. Which interpretations should guide the nurse’s report? Select all that apply.
options: Recent medicines and contrast exposure may help explain the change
A potassium result within range would exclude important renal impairment
A normal voiding frequency would show that the creatinine rise is insignificant
Urine volumes and fluid balance help characterize the current response
why: Potential renal stressors should be reported with the acute trend.
A potassium result alone cannot exclude renal impairment.
Frequency does not establish total output or negate the acute creatinine change.
Measured output and balance help describe renal and volume status alongside the laboratory trend.

items.assessment: New confusion with sodium122 warrants prompt neurological assessment/escalation; repeat sampling, rest or unilateral fluid treatment cannot replace timely assessment. No correction regimen is prescribed.

issues: Explicit6.7 result improves urgency, but removing it from handover is still conspicuously unreasonable. Use a plausible normal-clinical-observation misconception.

options: Wait for the routine morning laboratory draw because haemolysis usually raises potassium
Assess and urgently arrange verification with the team
Use a normal pulse rate to decide that the elevated value is an artefact
Treat the value as definitive without noting haemolysis
why: Possible artefact does not exclude dangerous true hyperkalaemia.
Assess promptly and urgently verify with the team; specimen quality affects interpretation.
A normal pulse rate does not exclude clinically important hyperkalaemia.
The haemolysis warning is relevant to verification and treatment decisions.

items.assessment: Prescribed therapeutic target plus bleeding assessment is the correct reference; untreated range, prior value alone and equating elevation with active bleeding are meaningful interpretive errors.

Symptomatic potassium2.9 makes cardiac rate/rhythm a defensible priority over detailed weakness, loss history or bowel motility. Item appropriately asks assessment priority rather than prescribing replacement.
Unclean collection with mixed flora supports discussing clean recollection; neither selecting one organism nor dismissing ongoing symptoms is justified.
Missing a timed void threatens validity; laboratory-directed restart is preferable to arbitrary interval extension or undisclosed incomplete submission.
Midstream timing and avoiding interior contact are appropriate independent-collection instructions. First-catch and inner-lid surface contamination are realistic technique errors.
Deep-cough recollection targets lower-respiratory material; pooling saliva or judging volume alone does not correct quality. Preparatory mouthwash remains test-instruction dependent.
Current-kit instructions govern collection and preparation; applying an old kit’s restrictions or switching to a generic container is a plausible but unsupported shortcut.

Prompt pretreatment culture collection is appropriate when it does not delay urgent antimicrobial care. Fever-peak, routine-visit and result-waiting delays are clinically meaningful sequencing errors.
Conflicting date of birth requires resolution before attribution; rechecking the name alone does not resolve identity. Repetitive name-only alternatives limit difficulty but no ambiguity is present.
Named result-review responsibility and a client contact route reduce pending-result loss. Documentation alone and interpreting silence as normal are common follow-up process failures.
Storage/time history must be checked with the laboratory; later refrigeration cannot erase an unrecorded delay. Freezing without instructions risks specimen integrity.

proposedChanges.stem: When reporting a clinically important laboratory change, which details most directly help the receiving clinician judge its urgency? Select all that apply.
options: The date of the next routine outpatient appointment
The client’s usual diet before admission
why: The client’s response and treatment context help establish urgency and possible causes.
A routine appointment date does not show how urgently the current change needs assessment.
Background diet may add context for some results, but current symptoms and the magnitude/rate of change more directly establish urgency.
Comparing values and times shows the magnitude and rate of change.
